# Timing

> "Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation."
>
> — 2 Corinthians 6:2

The habit is doing you no good, so the right time to stop is now. That much is obvious. Even so, timing deserves some thought.

The world treats porn as entertainment and masturbation as a faintly embarrassing pastime that hurts nobody. You know better by this point. For many men, getting caught by it at thirteen was the worst thing that happened to them, and they've never told anyone. It has quietly taken more from them than any enemy they could name. Something like that deserves to be dealt with properly, and dealing with it properly includes when.

## Your timetable {-}

In this book the "when" is simple. You stop when you finish the last chapter. (That is what the Introduction meant by stopping right away. There's no tapering and no ninety-day climb. You finish, and you stop.) The final step is a prayer, and you'll be ready for it. So you're not choosing a date so much as getting ready for one.

First, work out when the habit seems to matter most to you. If it's your pressure valve, the worst week at work will look like the wrong week. If it's your cure for boredom, the long empty holiday will. Know which sort you are, because that's where the Big Monster will try to bargain.

Next, look at the three weeks after you expect to finish. Is there a trip away on your own? Is your wife visiting her mother? Is there a woman you already know you shouldn't see? Are there exams, a deadline, a string of late nights in an empty house? None of these need put you off. They only need to be seen coming. A man who expects the quiet hotel room, and knows he's missing nothing in it, walks straight through it.

In the meantime, don't cut down. A ration only teaches you that being denied makes it precious. Carry on as you are, with one change: pay attention. Notice how it starts without your deciding. Notice the hunt, how short the end is and how flat the ten minutes after it are. Notice that nothing you were promised turned up. You're not looking for disgust. You're looking for the truth, and you've never watched before.

**WHATEVER YOU DO, DON'T TELL YOURSELF "NOT NOW, LATER" AND PUT THE BOOK IN A DRAWER. KEEP READING, KNOW ROUGHLY WHEN YOU'LL FINISH, AND LOOK FORWARD TO THAT DAY.**

Remember that you aren't giving anything up. You're about to be handed a great deal.

## Why the book doesn't say "stop today" {-}

The Big Monster isn't the same in any two men. One man has "I can't sleep without it", another has "I'll stop when I'm married", a third has "at least it isn't porn". That's why the types in the last few chapters look so different from one another, and why each man thinks his case is special.

A clever man can fall for a con. Only a fool keeps falling for it once he's seen how it's done. You're not a fool. You've just never been shown the trick.

This is why the book keeps to the instruction that annoys people: carry on as normal until the end. One pastor who has written on this habit gives the opposite advice: "I encourage you to stop masturbating immediately." We respect him, and stopping is where this book is taking you too. But consider what happens to most men who are told that on page one. Some never open the book. Others stop on the spot by willpower, feel deprived by Thursday, fall on Saturday, and conclude that this method doesn't work either.

There's a deeper reason. Everyone "knows" that quitting this is hard. And what does a man reach for when he faces something hard? His crutch. So quitting looks like a double blow. There's a hard job to do, and the one thing he leans on for hard jobs is taken away at the same moment. The strength of this method is that it doesn't work like that. It deals with the fears and the doubts first, while nothing has been taken from you. Then, when you do stop, you aren't starting a struggle. You're already free.

## The honest difficulty {-}

There is one honest difficulty with all this.

The gentle advice is the one above: know your trigger and choose a time when it's quiet. But that isn't the surest way. The surest way is to stop at the time you think is hardest. If the habit is your stress relief, stop in the worst week of the year. If it's your cure for loneliness, stop the week you're alone. Once you've proved you can enjoy life without it in the very situation you dreaded, every other situation is easy.

But if the book insisted on that, would you do it?

Every child knows there are two ways to take off a sticking plaster. You can peel it back a millimetre at a time, wincing, for a quarter of an hour. Or you can take hold of one corner and rip. Ripping is over before the sting arrives. Everybody knows it's better, and half of us still peel. If you told a peeler, "Rip it or leave it on for good," he'd leave it on until it grew into his arm.

Many men have used the gentle advice to put the day off. "Not this month, work's mad." "Not this month, I'm on holiday and I'd like to enjoy it." So I thought about making this chapter one word long:

**NOW.**

That really is the best advice there is. Would you follow it, though?

Here is the cleverest twist in the trap. When life is stressful, it's the wrong time to stop, because you "need" it. When life is calm, you feel no urgency, because things aren't so bad. One or the other is always true, so the right time never comes.

"He who observes the wind won't sow; and he who regards the clouds won't reap." (Ecclesiastes 11:4)

## Three questions about when {-}

1. The first time you did it, as a boy, did you decide you'd go on doing it for life, with no way of stopping? Of course you didn't.
2. Are you going to keep it up until you die? Will you be at it at sixty, and at seventy-five, a grandfather waiting for the house to empty? Of course you aren't.
3. Then when will you stop?

Tomorrow? After the exams? Next year? When you're married? Haven't you been asking that question since the day you first realised you couldn't leave it alone? Augustine asked it for years, and for years his answer was "not yet". Then one afternoon in a garden, sick of hearing himself say "tomorrow", he turned the question round: "Why not now? why not is there this hour an end to my uncleanness?"

Perhaps you're hoping to wake up one morning and find you've simply gone off it. Stop kidding yourself. The path across the lawn gets more worn each year you walk it. It doesn't grow over while you're still using it. Or are you waiting until it has cost you something you can't get back? A marriage, say, or a calling, or the best ten years of your working life? That would be a strange time to choose.

## "But my life is so stressful" {-}

The trap's last trick is the idea that today is the wrong day and tomorrow will be easier.

We tell ourselves we lead stressful lives. Compared with whom? You have a roof and a fridge, and a lock on the door. Nobody is hunting you. For most of us the day's danger is an inbox. Our great-grandfathers ploughed in the rain, buried children and went to war, and their stress was the real kind. God built human beings to carry far more than most of us are ever asked to. The frame you were given is strong.

When a man feels strong in mind and body, he enjoys the good days and gets through the bad ones. People confuse responsibility with stress. Responsibility only turns into stress when you don't feel up to it. And nothing makes a man feel less up to it than this habit. It drains him every night and tells him every morning that he can't keep his own word. Hard work and long hours don't break men, and nor does getting old. What breaks them is the false crutch they lean on to get through.

So look at it squarely.

You've already decided you're not staying in this trap for life. That means that at some point, easy or hard, you'll go through the business of getting free. It won't be easier next year. It will be the same job with another year of rut worn in. So the time is now, or as soon after now as finishing this book allows.

Think how fast a week goes. Think of the rest of your life with no locked door, no secret and nothing to confess for the hundredth time. And if you follow the instructions, you won't be gritting your teeth through the first weeks, waiting for it to get better. You'll find it easy, and you'll enjoy it.

Now is the acceptable time. Keep reading.
